constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never alone with another person' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The triggers, threat items, and memory content suggest a combat/military trauma pattern centered on environmental danger cues (fire, silence, shouting, sensory flashback phenomena), not an interpersonal danger pattern specifically involving being alone with another person. This strategy therefore appears to address a different trauma context than the one represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Feeling dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is more typically linked to sexual or severe interpersonal violation trauma. In this profile, the surrounding triggers, memory, and threat items point to a military combat-type danger formulation rather than contamination-based shame. Paired with the 'never alone with another person' strategy, it pulls the profile toward a different trauma meaning structure that is not otherwise represented.

vignette:
At 54, Marisol Alvarez had spent most of her adult life in the Army as a combat engineer, and she still talked about deployment in fragments rather than as a story with a beginning and end. The event she circled around happened during a route-clearance mission overseas, when an explosion ignited a vehicle ahead of hers. She remembered the sudden bloom of flames, the searing heat striking the exposed skin of her face and forearms, and men shouting over one another in the confusion. Those moments were preserved in sharp pieces rather than a narrative. She could not put them into a clear sequence even in the privacy of her own mind; what returned instead were flashes and sounds, especially the shouted commands and panic she heard that day.

Back home, those same sensory details became potent in ordinary life. At work, if she passed a training burn pit or caught sight of fire during demolition exercises, her body reacted before she could think. A burst of heat from industrial equipment against her skin or a soldier yelling across the motor pool could make her go rigid and instantly ready for danger. What unnerved her just as much was the silence that sometimes followed routine activity; an unusual quiet in a work area made her feel that something terrible was about to break loose. In those moments she was not only tense but unable to focus on what was in front of her. The trigger could also bring back the event whole and without warning, so that a smell of heat or the sight of flames was enough for her to hear the shouting in her head again as if she were back there.

Those sudden returns of memory shaped what she believed about herself and the world. Each time the scene intruded so forcefully, Marisol took it as proof that something was wrong with her, that other people could move on from war and she could not. She had come to believe the world was fundamentally dangerous, not just in combat but everywhere, and the randomness of what happened felt intolerably unfair to her. Seeing fire or hearing shouting did not simply startle her; it seemed to confirm that danger was always near and that she had been left to carry an injustice no one had put right. Over time she became sensitized to those cues themselves, scanning for heat, noise, and changes in the atmosphere as if her mind were teaching itself where the next threat would come from.

Her beliefs then began to govern how she lived. Because she was certain the world was dangerous and because she felt flawed for reacting so strongly, she tried to avoid anything that might be stressful. She turned down optional field exercises, lingered in administrative tasks when she could, and at home steered away from family cookouts where open flames and loud voices were likely. She worked hard to numb her feelings, speaking flatly when her husband asked what was wrong and trying to shut down whatever rose up inside her. She also checked her surroundings constantly, in the office, on base, in parking lots, noticing exits, listening for changes in sound, looking for anything that might signal threat. That constant management of herself made her feel even more unlike the person she used to be, reinforcing her conviction that there was something defective in her.

The memories themselves fed this pattern. Because they arrived without warning and brought the shouting back so vividly, Marisol began organizing her days around not being caught off guard. She avoided stressors and kept herself emotionally blunted because she feared that any strong feeling would open the door to the full memory. Yet the more she lived in this narrowed, watchful way, the more tense her body remained. She was on alert so much of the time that concentration became difficult even during routine engineering planning, and once she was already keyed up, the next silence, shout, or wave of heat struck with even more force. Hypervigilance made the memories easier to set off; the memories intensified her sense of present threat.

Over months this tightened into the life she now found herself living. Her constant scanning meant she noticed every flare, every raised voice, every change in temperature, which made those triggers feel omnipresent. Avoiding stress and numbing herself had shrunk her world but had not made it feel safer. Instead, the restrictions seemed to prove that the world really was dangerous and that she really was damaged by what had happened. Her marriage had grown strained by her distance, and at work she was ashamed that she could no longer concentrate as she once had in the very environment where she was expected to lead calmly.

Marisol finally came for help after freezing during a stateside training exercise when flames rose unexpectedly and someone shouted for equipment. She recovered quickly enough that others may not have understood what happened, but she spent the rest of the day convinced she could hear the old voices in her head. What frightened her most was not just the memory itself but the sense that her life had become organized around waiting for it. She said she wanted, more than anything, to be able to stand in her own work environment without feeling that danger was already there, and to understand whether the part of her that felt permanently wrong could still be reached.
